title: Many Young Adults Don't Have DIY Skills — Survey
paragraphs: Can you change a light bulb, put up a shelf or fix a dripping tap? According to recent surveys in the UK, many young adults do not feel confident doing these kinds of jobs around the home.

In one survey, Nationwide Building Society asked more than 2,000 people about their DIY skills in September 2025. DIY means "do it yourself," and it refers to repairing or improving your home without paying a professional. The survey found that 41% of people in Gen Z, aged 16 to 28, were not confident about their practical skills. Only 9% of Gen Z had ever bled a radiator, which means letting air out of a heater, compared with 53% of baby boomers.

Another survey, by the car and bike shop Halfords, asked 2,000 people in the UK about practical tasks. It found that one in five people aged 18 to 27 did not know what a spanner was. One in five said they would call a professional to change a ceiling light bulb. On average, people in this age group spent £1,300 a year paying professionals to do jobs they could probably do themselves. Halfords calls this trend "GOTDIT," which stands for "get others to do it."

Why is this happening? In the Nationwide survey, the most common reason given was that knowledge is not being passed down from parents to children. Others said that practical skills are not seen as important anymore, or that it is easy to pay a professional.
Many young people now learn DIY online. According to Nationwide, YouTube is the most popular place to find help, and TikTok is popular among Gen Z.

However, there is some good news. When young people do start a DIY job, they finish it faster than older people. On average, Gen Z leaves jobs unfinished for three to four months, compared with 11 months for baby boomers.
